q-suetonius-vare: Suetonius (Augustus 23) says the emperor let his hair and beard grow and kept the day of the disaster as a day of mourning. The legion numbers XVII, XVIII and XIX were never used again. Note the vocative Vāre and the imperative redde.
q-seneca-docent: Seneca wrote 124 letters to Lucilius in his last years, around AD 62–65, as practical lessons in Stoic living. This line, from Letter 7, is a neat example of dum + present: 'while they teach'.
q-seneca-aliena: Seneca's point is that we guard our money but waste our hours, the only thing that is truly ours. Notice tantum, 'only', and the vocative Lūcīlī.
q-martial-bona: Martial (c. AD 40–104), from Bilbilis in Spain, published fifteen books of short, sharp epigrams about life in Rome. The repeated sunt shows how Latin builds a list by simply restating the verb.
i-pompeii-felices: More than 10,000 inscriptions survive from Pompeii, preserved when Vesuvius buried the town in AD 79. Valeāmus is a subjunctive of wish, 'may we be well', from the same verb as valē, 'goodbye'.
q-cicero-salus: The line comes from On the Laws (3.8), written in the 50s BC. It has been used since as a motto by states and politicians, from John Locke's writings to the state of Missouri. Estō is an old future imperative, 'let it be'.
q-tacitus-solitudinem: Calgacus' speech in the Agricola is one of the sharpest critiques of empire in Latin, written by a Roman about his own father-in-law's campaign. Tacitus probably composed the words himself, as ancient historians often did with speeches.
i-pantheon-agrippa: Agrippa, Augustus' right-hand man, built the first Pantheon in 27–25 BC; the present building with its huge unreinforced concrete dome is Hadrian's. COS TERTIVM means 'consul for the third time', and FECIT, 'made', is the perfect tense.
i-pompeii-cave: The House of the Tragic Poet was excavated in 1824 and is named after a mosaic of actors inside. Cavē is the imperative of cavēre, 'to beware'; canem is the accusative of canis, 'dog'.
i-pompeii-romula: Graffiti like this were scratched into wall plaster with a stylus or nail. Hīc means 'here', and morārī, 'to linger, stay', is a deponent verb: passive in form, active in meaning.
q-martial-sabidi: The epigram (1.32) works because Martial never gives a reason: the only reason is that he can't give one. The infinitive dīcere depends on possum, a structure you will see constantly.
q-terence-homo: Terence (died c. 159 BC), a former slave from North Africa, adapted Greek comedies for Roman audiences; this line is from The Self-Tormentor (163 BC). Writers from Cicero to Montaigne and Maya Angelou quoted it.
q-caesar-belgae: The sentence comes from the very first chapter of Caesar's Gallic War (1.1), written as a third-person report of his campaigns of 58–50 BC. Fortissimī is a superlative: fortis, fortior, fortissimus.
q-horace-modus: The line is Satires 1.1.106, written in the 30s BC. Horace's ideal of the 'golden mean' (aurea mediocritās, Odes 2.10) runs through all his work. Note the parallel est … sunt.
q-virgil-timeo: The line is Aeneid 2.49. Laocoön's death, crushed with his sons by serpents, is the subject of the famous marble group now in the Vatican Museums. Danaōs is a poetic name for the Greeks, and et here means 'even'.
q-tacitus-urbem: These are the first words of Tacitus' Annals, written c. AD 115–120, covering the emperors from Tiberius to Nero. Habuēre is a short form of habuērunt, 'they had'.
q-juvenal-mens: The line is from Satire 10 (line 356), written in the early 2nd century AD. Juvenal goes on to list a brave heart that does not fear death. Ōrandum est is a gerundive: 'it must be prayed'.
i-sttl: S·T·T·L stands for sit tibi terra levis, 'may the earth be light on you'. D·M, Dīs Mānibus, 'to the spirits of the dead', opens thousands of Roman tombstones. Abbreviations like these are the first thing to learn when reading inscriptions.
q-ovid-urbis: The Fasti, a poem on the Roman calendar, covers January to June; Terminus' festival, the Terminalia, fell on 23 February (Fasti 2.684). The pun works because urbs, 'city', and orbis, 'world', sound alike.
q-catullus-ave: Poem 101 was probably written when Catullus visited his brother's grave in the Troad (north-west Turkey) around 57 BC. Avē atque valē, 'hail and farewell', were the ritual words spoken to the dead.
i-titus-spqr: The Arch of Titus stands on the Via Sacra at the edge of the Roman Forum and was finished after AD 81. DIVO TITO is dative: the arch is dedicated 'to the deified Titus', son of the deified Vespasian.
q-catullus-odi: Poem 85 is an elegiac couplet. 'Lesbia' is usually identified with Clodia, a noblewoman of the Claudian family. Excrucior, the last word, is passive: 'I am tortured', literally 'crucified'.
q-horace-dulce: The line is Odes 3.2.13, from a group of six poems that praise the old Roman virtues promoted under Augustus. Morī, 'to die', is a deponent infinitive and acts as the subject: 'to die is sweet'.
q-virgil-moenia: Virgil wrote the Aeneid between about 29 and 19 BC; this is line 1.7. Alba Longa was said to have been founded by Aeneas' son Ascanius, and Romulus and Remus descended from its kings.
q-plautus-lupus: Plautus (c. 254–184 BC) wrote the comedy The Donkeys (Asinaria, line 495), one of the oldest surviving Latin texts. The philosopher Thomas Hobbes made homo homini lupus famous in the 17th century.
q-virgil-forsan: The line is Aeneid 1.203. Aeneas hides his own worry and speaks hope to his men, a model of the leader's duty. Meminisse, 'to remember', is a perfect-form infinitive with present meaning.
q-seneca-vindica: This is Letter 1.1. Seneca was Nero's tutor and adviser and was forced to kill himself in AD 65. Vindicā is an imperative from vindicāre, a legal word for claiming property or freeing a slave.
q-resgestae-annos: The text was copied onto temples across the empire; the best surviving copy is on the Temple of Augustus and Rome in Ankara, Turkey. Annōs ūndēvīgintī nātus means literally 'born nineteen years'.
q-seneca-prope: This is Letter 41. Seneca's idea of a divine spark within each person is Stoic; Christian writers later found it close to their own thinking. Prope, tēcum and intus pile up three ways of saying 'near'.
i-spqr: The phrase dates from the Republic and was carried on legionary standards and public buildings throughout Roman history. Populusque joins populus with -que, 'and', attached to the second word.
q-terence-quot: The line comes from Terence's Phormio (line 454), staged in 161 BC. Cicero also quoted it. Quot … tot is a pair of correlatives: 'as many … so many'.
q-cornelia-ornamenta: Cornelia, daughter of Scipio Africanus, raised her sons Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, both later reforming tribunes. Valerius Maximus (4.4) tells the story, and she became the Roman model of the ideal mother.
i-pompeii-fullones: Fullers cleaned and finished woollen cloth using water and urine, so laundries were noisy, smelly working places. The joke works because readers knew Arma virumque canō by heart.
q-virgil-tantaene: The line is Aeneid 1.11. Juno hated the Trojans because of the judgment of Paris and because she favoured Carthage, which Rome was fated to destroy. -ne turns the line into a question.
q-ovid-vesta: The line is Fasti 6.267. The round temple of Vesta still partly stands in the Forum; the Vestals had to keep its fire alight, and letting it go out was a terrible omen.
q-horace-sapere: These lines are Epistles 1.2.40. Sapere aude, 'dare to be wise', later became the motto of the Enlightenment through Immanuel Kant's essay of 1784.
q-virgil-regere: These lines are Aeneid 6.851–853. Anchises adds that Rome should 'spare the defeated and war down the proud', parcere subiectīs et dēbellāre superbōs. Mementō is the imperative of meminī, 'remember'.
q-virgil-arma: These are the first words of the Aeneid. The poem is written in dactylic hexameter, the metre of Homer, and was a school text across the Roman world and the Middle Ages. Canō, 'I sing', is first person present.
q-terence-fortis: The proverb comes from Terence's Phormio (line 203). Virgil has a version, audentēs fortūna iuvat (Aeneid 10.284), and Pliny the Younger says his uncle quoted it as he sailed towards Vesuvius in AD 79. Fortīs is an older spelling of the accusative plural fortēs.
i-rib-facilis: The stone (RIB 200) was found in 1868 and is now in Colchester Castle Museum. Facilis served in the Twentieth Legion; the stone names the two freedmen, Verecundus and Novicius, who set it up.
q-virgil-fugit: The line is Georgics 3.284, from Virgil's four-book poem on farming (c. 29 BC). Irreparābile means 'that cannot be recovered'. Fugit is repeated for emphasis, a figure called anaphora.
q-seneca-nusquam: This is Letter 2.2. Seneca advises Lucilius to read deeply in a few good authors rather than a little of everything. Quī ubīque est, 'the one who is everywhere', is a relative clause acting as the subject.
q-cicero-historia: The line is On the Orator 2.36, written in 55 BC. Cicero's full list calls history the witness of the times, light of truth, life of memory, teacher of life and messenger of antiquity.
q-virgil-musa: The line is Aeneid 1.8. Like Homer, Virgil opens by calling on the Muse. Memorā is an imperative: 'tell, recall'. Mihi is dative, 'to me'.
q-virgil-facilis: These lines are Aeneid 6.126–129. Avernus, a crater lake near Naples, was believed to be an entrance to the underworld. The phrase facilis dēscēnsus Avernō is still used for any easy slide into trouble.
q-ovid-gutta: These lines are from Letters from the Black Sea (Ex Ponto 4.10.5). Augustus exiled Ovid in AD 8 to Tomis, now Constanța in Romania, for 'a poem and a mistake'; he died there.
i-rib-flavinus: Flavinus served in the cavalry regiment ala Petriana; his stone (RIB 1172) dates to the late 1st century AD. Images of a rider trampling a fallen enemy were a standard design for Roman cavalry tombstones.
i-pompeii-successus: The graffito was found in a house in Pompeii. Graffiti like this show the everyday Latin of shopkeepers and workers, including spelling mistakes that reveal how the language was actually spoken.
c-brutus-eidmar: EID MAR is short for Eīdibus Mārtiīs, 'on the Ides of March', 15 March 44 BC. The cap (pilleus) was given to freed slaves, so the coin claims the murder freed Rome. Only about a hundred of these coins are known.
c-octavian-aegypto: The coins carry the legend AEGVPTO CAPTA, an ablative absolute: 'Egypt having been captured'. Antony and Cleopatra died in 30 BC after their defeat at Actium the year before.
q-catullus-vivamus: Vīvāmus and amēmus are subjunctives of exhortation: 'let us live, let us love'. The poem (Catullus 5) goes on to demand a thousand kisses, then a hundred, then a thousand more.
q-ovid-expedit: The line is Art of Love 1.637. Ovid's playful, irreverent love poetry may have been part of the reason Augustus banished him. Expedit, 'it is useful', is an impersonal verb.
q-seneca-differtur: The line is Letter 1.3. Seneca's point is that delay is the greatest waste of life. Differtur is passive, 'it is put off'; dum means 'while'.
q-cicero-cedant: The line is from Cicero's poem On His Consulship, quoted in On Duties (1.77). It celebrates how he crushed Catiline's conspiracy in 63 BC as a civilian. Cedant is a subjunctive of wish: 'let them yield'.
q-cicero-quousque: Cicero gave the speech on 8 November 63 BC in the Temple of Jupiter Stator; Catiline left Rome that night. Abūtēre is a future second-person form of the deponent abūtor, 'abuse'.
q-suetonius-alea: The Rubicon was a small river marking the boundary between Cisalpine Gaul and Italy; bringing an army across it was treason. Iacta est is a perfect passive: 'has been thrown'. Ālea is a die, as in a game of dice.
q-virgil-tantae: This is Aeneid 1.33, the line that ends Virgil's opening section. Mōlis is genitive with tantae: '(a matter) of so great effort'. Condere means 'to found', as in ab urbe conditā.
q-juvenal-panem: The line is Satire 10.81. Free grain and chariot races in the Circus Maximus were indeed how emperors kept the city crowd content. Circēnsēs means 'circus games'.
q-lucretius-religio: The line is On the Nature of Things 1.101, from the 50s BC. Lucretius wanted to free readers from fear of the gods and death by explaining the world as atoms and void. Potuit, 'was able', takes the infinitive suādēre.
q-ovid-edax: These lines are Metamorphoses 15.234. The poem, finished around AD 8, tells about 250 myths of transformation. Edāx, 'devouring', comes from edere, 'to eat'.
q-livy-vae: Livy tells the story in his history of Rome (5.48). The Gallic sack, around 390 BC, left the Romans with a lasting fear of invasion. Vae victīs: vae, 'woe', takes the dative, 'to the conquered'.
q-horace-exegi: This is Odes 3.30.1, written about 23 BC. Exēgī is the perfect of exigō, 'I have completed'. Aere perennius uses a comparative with the ablative: 'more lasting than bronze'.
i-pompeii-admiror: The couplet (CIL IV 1904 and copies) is a joke that the wall has not collapsed under the weight of so many writers' 'boredom'. Admīror is a deponent verb: passive form, active meaning.
i-rib-regina: The stone (RIB 1065), from the late 2nd century AD, shows Regina seated with her spindle and jewellery box. Her husband Barates came from Palmyra in Syria, showing how far people travelled across the empire.
